note: The machine-readable half of docs/art/ASSET-SPEC.md's budget section. Every number here is either measured from a named on-disk source or explicitly marked provisional. tests/asset-budget.test.mjs enforces it and fails when the prose and this file disagree.

baseline.measuredBy: npm run build, then tools/asset-budget.mjs measure
baseline.sourcemapNote: package.json build.files excludes dist/**/*.map, so sourcemaps are built but never shipped and are excluded from every ceiling below.

ceilings.shippedTotalWhy: 205 MiB = the 2.25 MiB code ceiling plus the 200 MiB asset allowance plus slack. Arithmetically downstream of assetBytes, and re-derived with it: the original 24 MiB was justified by a cold-download time that Steam-only distribution retired.
ceilings.codeWhy: 2.25 MiB = the 1.85 MiB measured code baseline plus ~22% growth headroom: ordinary feature work will not trip it, a doubling or an accidentally-bundled dependency will. UNCHANGED by the Steam re-derivation — bundle bloat and dependency creep have nothing to do with the distribution channel.
ceilings.electronRuntimeWhy: 348 MiB, measured at node_modules/electron/dist for the pinned Electron 43.3.0. Not a ceiling — the reference magnitude the asset ceiling is set against, since electron-builder ships this unpacked (asar: false, win/dir) and it dominates what a player actually downloads from Steam. tools/asset-budget.mjs never measures it.
ceilings.assetWhy: 200 MiB, the HARD ceiling under Steam-only distribution (settled 2026-08-14). The former 20 MiB defended a ~20 s cold download on a 10 Mbit line — a web-delivery argument that does not survive shipping through SteamPipe beside a 348 MiB Electron runtime. 200 MiB sits about half an order of magnitude below that runtime: large enough that ordinary PBR/mesh/HDRI work never trips it, small enough that a wholesale pack forces a re-chunking conversation. Derived blind (no knowledge of any candidate's weight) so the number is not a rationalisation of what happened to be shortlisted.
ceilings.formerAssetWhy: The pre-Steam 20 MiB ceiling, kept so the spec's prose can cite the number it replaced without the stray-figure sweep reading the citation as drift. Not enforced.
ceilings.assetReviewWhy: 25 MiB, the SOFT review threshold. Warns, never fails. The original 20 MiB ceiling's real job was stated in its own text — to make adopting a large pack 'a decision rather than a purchase' — and that is a review policy, not a technical limit. A correct hard ceiling that nothing plausible can trip would silently stop doing that job, which is this repo's characteristic guard-passes-while-blind shape. So the two jobs get two numbers: 200 MiB breaks the build, 25 MiB requires a written note on the adopting issue.
ceilings.vramWhy: PROVISIONAL. No atlas-scale VRAM reasoning exists in this repo to derive from, so 512 MiB is set as the resident-texture headroom that keeps the game inside a 2 GB shared-memory integrated adapter alongside the framebuffer and post stack. Replace it with a measured figure when one exists. The two checkable proxies below stand in for it meanwhile.
ceilings.gpuProxyWhy: Texture and geometry counts from the capture manifest's perf block are the only committed VRAM-adjacent measurements that exist; 96/900 is roughly +80%/+29% over the 53/700 baseline, sized so an asset pack landing wholesale is visible before a VRAM measurement exists.

frameTime.why: A CEILING, not a band. The documented '21-26 ms band' does not survive contact with the record: the committed perf runs report combat-24 medians of 16.9, 18.6, 20.0, 20.5, 21.8, 20.5 and 24.5 ms, so five of seven sit below the band's lower bound and a lower bound would fail runs that got faster. 26.0 ms keeps the documented upper bound; p95 32.0 ms sits just above the worst recorded p95 (27.1 ms) plus the run-to-run spread the same record shows.
frameTime.toleranceWhy: The record's own medians span 16.9-24.5 ms on one machine across one tree family — roughly +/-19% around the midpoint — so any ceiling tighter than about +25% over the latest recorded median (20.5 ms) would flap on run noise rather than on regressions. 26.0 ms is +27%.
frameTime.historicalWhy: The review-prose medians the whys above cite, kept here so the spec's historical citations stay allowlisted by the stray-figure sweep even as the live frameTimeRecord is re-measured and its numbers move.
